To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
perinatal fluoxetine exposure increases the rewarding effects of cocaine and decreases the reinforcing properties of cocaine in rats.
perinatal fluoexetine exposure alters adult neural substrates and behaviors associated with the reinforcing effects of cocaine in male Wistar rat offspring.
perinatal antidepressant exposure produces a positive hedonics shift for conditioned reinforcing properties of cocaine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neurobehavioral consequences of perinatally administered fluoxetine on offspring drug‐seeking and drug‐reward behaviors.
the effects of perinatal exposure of rats to fluoxetine, the most widely prescribed selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant.
how the brain is affected by exposure to antidepressants during the prenatal period.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the data presented in this paper suggest that perinatally administered fluoxetine produces long‐lasting changes in serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission in the brain and produces long‐lasting effects on the reinforcing properties of cocaine in adult offspring.

prenatal fluoxetine exposure alters the neural circuitry of the brain and produces a positive shift in the reinforcing properties of cocaine in adult offspring, and this effect is likely to be mediated via a serotoninergic mechanism.
perinatal fluvoxamine exposure produces an increase in adult drug self-administration, but only in the presence of a positive hedonic bias for cocaine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the offspring of rats exposed to fluoxetine in the womb have a greater preference for cocaine and take more cocaine when given the chance.
prenatal exposure to fluoxetine (SSRI) can cause long-term behavioral and neurochemical alterations in the developing brain of the offspring.

perinatal fluoexetine exposure produces a significant decrease in serotonin transporter‐like immunoactivity in the rapah nuclei, and an increase in conditioned place preference for cocaine, and an increased rate of extinction of cocaine self‐administration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of maternal antidepressants on the developing brain are not limited to the serotonin system.

antidepressant exposure during development can produce a positive shift in hedonic valence for cocaine in adult rats, which may contribute to the high prevalence of comorbidity between depression and substance use disorders.
the effects of perinatal exposure on offspring behavior are not necessarily limited to a single drug.
